newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Analysts split on reason for Irish fx intervention.
newsitem.headline: Analysts split on reason for Irish fx intervention.

text.p: Analysts agree that central bank intervention may have been behind an across-the-board drop in the value of the Irish pound earlier this week but are less certain about the reasons behind the central bank move.
Some believe the bank acted to prevent a "green pound" revaluation putting further pressure on a BSE-battered farming sector but others dispute this.
The Irish pound slipped below 1.03 sterling last Monday, falling to 1.0293 from 1.0304 on Friday.
It also lost ground against the mark, dollar and French franc, while the trade-weighted index dropped to 68.71 from 68.79.

The central bank has a policy of not commenting on intervention. But analysts believe the bank must have been in the market selling the Irish pound as it dropped at a time when there was heavy overseas buying of Irish government bonds, driven by the prospect of EMU convergence.
"On Friday and Monday the Irish pound pretty much eased back against all the main currencies in an across the board move.
"We know that there was big foreign buying of the bond market so the implication there is that it was intervention," said Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers.
Some analysts believe the intervention was designed to ward off a threatened revaluation of the green pound, the money which is paid to farmers in EU intervention subsidies.
"The timing of it makes it look quite likely because effectively a revaluation of the green pound was triggered last week," said Han de Jong, economist at Goodbody Stockbrokers.

The Irish Co-operative Organisation Society (ICOS) warned last week that the strength of the Irish pound against the basket of currencies making up the Ecu could trigger a revaluation of the green pound, costing the Irish food sector up to 60 million punts a year.
But others believe the bank would be unlikely to intervene to help one interest group.

"I don't think the central bank determines exchange rate policy on that basis. As I understand it there is a question mark right now as to whether or not the green pound will be revalued but I think it's coincidental," NCB's O'Brien said.

He said the main aims of the central bank's currency policy were to keep the Irish pound trading comfortably against the mark in the ERM and to ensure the trade-weighted index remained strong enough to keep a lid on inflation.
"With the exchange rate configuration where the central bank wants it but with strong overseas buying of the market pushing it higher, why wouldn't the bank intervene?" O'Brien said.

But de Jong believes the bank took temporary action to help the farmers until it can decide whether dollar and sterling strength, the main factors driving the Irish pound higher, is likely to persist or not.

"You cannot ignore the fact that farmers will face more severe problems if the green pound is revalued and if the central bank can avoid that by taking a little bit of action now, it may be worth the effort," he said.
